claim: The nucleus incertus (NI) is a conserved hindbrain structure implicated in the stress response, arousal, and memory.
source: The nucleus incertus (NI), a conserved hindbrain structure implicated in the stress response, arousal, and memory, is a major site for production of the neuropeptide relaxin-3.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature establishing these functional roles

claim: The nucleus incertus is a major site for production of the neuropeptide relaxin-3.
source: The nucleus incertus (NI), a conserved hindbrain structure implicated in the stress response, arousal, and memory, is a major site for production of the neuropeptide relaxin-3.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: A neuronal cluster defined by goosecoid homeobox 2 (gsc2) expression lies adjacent to relaxin 3a (rln3a) neurons in the zebrafish analogue of the NI.
source: On the basis of goosecoid homeobox 2 (gsc2) expression, we identified a neuronal cluster that lies adjacent to relaxin 3a (rln3a) neurons in the zebrafish analogue of the NI.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1

claim: gsc2 and rln3a NI neurons differ in their efferent and afferent connectivity.
source: we used CRISPR/Cas9 targeted integration to drive gene expression specifically in each neuronal group, and found that they differ in their efferent and afferent connectivity, spontaneous activity, and functional properties.
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figures 4 and 5

claim: gsc2 and rln3a NI neurons differ in their spontaneous activity.
source: we used CRISPR/Cas9 targeted integration to drive gene expression specifically in each neuronal group, and found that they differ in their efferent and afferent connectivity, spontaneous activity, and functional properties.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7

claim: gsc2 and rln3a NI neurons differ in their functional properties.
source: we used CRISPR/Cas9 targeted integration to drive gene expression specifically in each neuronal group, and found that they differ in their efferent and afferent connectivity, spontaneous activity, and functional properties.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8

claim: gsc2 and rln3a NI neurons have widely divergent projection patterns.
source: gsc2 and rln3a NI neurons have widely divergent projection patterns and innervate distinct subregions of the midbrain interpeduncular nucleus (IPN).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figures 4 and 5

claim: gsc2 and rln3a NI neurons innervate distinct subregions of the midbrain interpeduncular nucleus (IPN).
source: gsc2 and rln3a NI neurons have widely divergent projection patterns and innervate distinct subregions of the midbrain interpeduncular nucleus (IPN).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5

claim: gsc2 neurons are activated more robustly by electric shock than rln3a neurons.
source: Whereas gsc2 neurons are activated more robustly by electric shock, rln3a neurons exhibit spontaneous fluctuations in calcium signaling and regulate locomotor activity.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7

claim: rln3a neurons exhibit spontaneous fluctuations in calcium signaling.
source: Whereas gsc2 neurons are activated more robustly by electric shock, rln3a neurons exhibit spontaneous fluctuations in calcium signaling and regulate locomotor activity.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7

claim: rln3a neurons regulate locomotor activity.
source: Whereas gsc2 neurons are activated more robustly by electric shock, rln3a neurons exhibit spontaneous fluctuations in calcium signaling and regulate locomotor activity.
evidence: Supported by ablation and behavioral data shown in Figure 8

claim: The nucleus incertus was originally identified in the human brain by Streeter in 1903.
source: The nucleus incertus (NI), originally identified in the human brain (Streeter, 1903), consists of bilaterally paired clusters of neurons at the midline of the floor of the fourth ventricle (Ma and Gundlach, 2015; Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Streeter, 1903

claim: The nucleus incertus consists of bilaterally paired clusters of neurons at the midline of the floor of the fourth ventricle.
source: The nucleus incertus (NI), originally identified in the human brain (Streeter, 1903), consists of bilaterally paired clusters of neurons at the midline of the floor of the fourth ventricle (Ma and Gundlach, 2015; Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma and Gundlach, 2015; Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2018

claim: Cholecystokinin has been detected in the nucleus incertus region.
source: A variety of neuropeptides have been detected in the region, including cholecystokinin (Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003), neuromedin B (Lu et al., 2020), neurotensin (Jennes et al., 1982), and relaxin-3 (Burazin et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2010); however, the properties of NI neuronal subtypes are not well defined.
evidence: Supported by citation to Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003

claim: Neuromedin B has been detected in the nucleus incertus region.
source: A variety of neuropeptides have been detected in the region, including cholecystokinin (Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003), neuromedin B (Lu et al., 2020), neurotensin (Jennes et al., 1982), and relaxin-3 (Burazin et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2010); however, the properties of NI neuronal subtypes are not well defined.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2020

claim: Neurotensin has been detected in the nucleus incertus region.
source: A variety of neuropeptides have been detected in the region, including cholecystokinin (Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003), neuromedin B (Lu et al., 2020), neurotensin (Jennes et al., 1982), and relaxin-3 (Burazin et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2010); however, the properties of NI neuronal subtypes are not well defined.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jennes et al., 1982

claim: Relaxin-3 has been detected in the nucleus incertus region.
source: A variety of neuropeptides have been detected in the region, including cholecystokinin (Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003), neuromedin B (Lu et al., 2020), neurotensin (Jennes et al., 1982), and relaxin-3 (Burazin et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2010); however, the properties of NI neuronal subtypes are not well defined.
evidence: Supported by citations to Burazin et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2010

claim: The properties of NI neuronal subtypes are not well defined.
source: A variety of neuropeptides have been detected in the region, including cholecystokinin (Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003), neuromedin B (Lu et al., 2020), neurotensin (Jennes et al., 1982), and relaxin-3 (Burazin et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2010); however, the properties of NI neuronal subtypes are not well defined.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: NI neurons are enriched in receptors for the Corticotropin Releasing Factor (CRF).
source: Initial investigations in rodents indicate that the NI responds to stressful cues; NI neurons are enriched in receptors for the Corticotropin Releasing Factor (CRF) and upregulate c-Fos in response to CRF exposure (Bittencourt and Sawchenko, 2000; Potter et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bittencourt and Sawchenko, 2000; Potter et al., 1994

claim: NI neurons upregulate c-Fos in response to CRF exposure.
source: Initial investigations in rodents indicate that the NI responds to stressful cues; NI neurons are enriched in receptors for the Corticotropin Releasing Factor (CRF) and upregulate c-Fos in response to CRF exposure (Bittencourt and Sawchenko, 2000; Potter et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bittencourt and Sawchenko, 2000; Potter et al., 1994

claim: Placement in an elevated plus maze induces expression of c-Fos in the NI.
source: Placement in an elevated plus maze, exposure to an anxiogenic drug, foot shock, or water-restraint stress also induce expression of the neural activity marker c-Fos in the NI (Lawther et al., 2015; Passerin et al., 2000; Rajkumar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lawther et al., 2015; Passerin et al., 2000; Rajkumar et al., 2016

claim: Exposure to an anxiogenic drug induces expression of c-Fos in the NI.
source: Placement in an elevated plus maze, exposure to an anxiogenic drug, foot shock, or water-restraint stress also induce expression of the neural activity marker c-Fos in the NI (Lawther et al., 2015; Passerin et al., 2000; Rajkumar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lawther et al., 2015; Passerin et al., 2000; Rajkumar et al., 2016

claim: Foot shock induces expression of c-Fos in the NI.
source: Placement in an elevated plus maze, exposure to an anxiogenic drug, foot shock, or water-restraint stress also induce expression of the neural activity marker c-Fos in the NI (Lawther et al., 2015; Passerin et al., 2000; Rajkumar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lawther et al., 2015; Passerin et al., 2000; Rajkumar et al., 2016

claim: Water-restraint stress induces expression of c-Fos in the NI.
source: Placement in an elevated plus maze, exposure to an anxiogenic drug, foot shock, or water-restraint stress also induce expression of the neural activity marker c-Fos in the NI (Lawther et al., 2015; Passerin et al., 2000; Rajkumar et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lawther et al., 2015; Passerin et al., 2000; Rajkumar et al., 2016

claim: Electrical microstimulation of the NI promotes locomotion in rats.
source: For example, electrical microstimulation of the NI promotes locomotion in rats (Farooq et al., 2016), and optogenetic activation of a subset of neurons in the mouse NI that produce the neuropeptide neuromedin B increases locomotor speed (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Farooq et al., 2016

claim: Optogenetic activation of neuromedin B-producing neurons in the mouse NI increases locomotor speed.
source: For example, electrical microstimulation of the NI promotes locomotion in rats (Farooq et al., 2016), and optogenetic activation of a subset of neurons in the mouse NI that produce the neuropeptide neuromedin B increases locomotor speed (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2020

claim: In rodents, the NI contains the largest population of neurons in the brain that produce relaxin-3 (RLN3).
source: In rodents, the NI contains the largest population of neurons in the brain that produce relaxin-3 (RLN3; Smith et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2005), a neuropeptide thought to mediate behavioral responses to aversive stimuli (Lawther et al., 2015; Ryan et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2005

claim: Relaxin-3 is a neuropeptide thought to mediate behavioral responses to aversive stimuli.
source: In rodents, the NI contains the largest population of neurons in the brain that produce relaxin-3 (RLN3; Smith et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2005), a neuropeptide thought to mediate behavioral responses to aversive stimuli (Lawther et al., 2015; Ryan et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lawther et al., 2015; Ryan et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2015

claim: There are NI neurons that do not produce RLN3.
source: Although there are also NI neurons that do not produce RLN3 (Ma et al., 2013), their characteristics are not well distinguished from the RLN3 population.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma et al., 2013

claim: The characteristics of non-RLN3 NI neurons are not well distinguished from the RLN3 population.
source: Although there are also NI neurons that do not produce RLN3 (Ma et al., 2013), their characteristics are not well distinguished from the RLN3 population.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Larval zebrafish transparency is advantageous for monitoring and manipulating specific subpopulations.
source: Larval zebrafish are a powerful model to investigate neuronal diversity and connectivity because their transparency and genetic tractability are advantageous for monitoring and manipulating specific subpopulations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish as a model organism

claim: Larval zebrafish genetic tractability is advantageous for monitoring and manipulating specific subpopulations.
source: Larval zebrafish are a powerful model to investigate neuronal diversity and connectivity because their transparency and genetic tractability are advantageous for monitoring and manipulating specific subpopulations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrafish as a model organism

claim: In zebrafish, the presumed analogue of the NI is the griseum centrale.
source: In zebrafish, the presumed analogue of the NI is the griseum centrale, situated on the ventral surface of the rhombencephalic ventricle (Agetsuma et al., 2010; Olson et al., 2017; Wullimann et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Agetsuma et al., 2010; Olson et al., 2017; Wullimann et al., 1996

claim: The griseum centrale is situated on the ventral surface of the rhombencephalic ventricle.
source: In zebrafish, the presumed analogue of the NI is the griseum centrale, situated on the ventral surface of the rhombencephalic ventricle (Agetsuma et al., 2010; Olson et al., 2017; Wullimann et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Agetsuma et al., 2010; Olson et al., 2017; Wullimann et al., 1996

claim: Expression of relaxin 3a (rln3a) is restricted to two bilaterally paired clusters of neurons in the midbrain and two bilaterally paired nuclei bordering the hindbrain midline.
source: Expression of relaxin 3a (rln3a) is restricted to two bilaterally paired clusters of neurons in the midbrain and two bilaterally paired nuclei bordering the hindbrain midline (Donizetti et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Donizetti et al., 2008

claim: The midbrain rln3a expression domains correspond to the periaqueductal gray (PAG).
source: It was proposed that the midbrain rln3a expression domains correspond to the periaqueductal gray (PAG), a region that produces RLN3 in rodents (Ma et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 2005), and that the hindbrain rln3a neuronal clusters correspond to the NI (Donizetti et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 2005; Donizetti et al., 2008

claim: The periaqueductal gray (PAG) produces RLN3 in rodents.
source: It was proposed that the midbrain rln3a expression domains correspond to the periaqueductal gray (PAG), a region that produces RLN3 in rodents (Ma et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 2005), and that the hindbrain rln3a neuronal clusters correspond to the NI (Donizetti et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 2005

claim: The hindbrain rln3a neuronal clusters correspond to the NI.
source: It was proposed that the midbrain rln3a expression domains correspond to the periaqueductal gray (PAG), a region that produces RLN3 in rodents (Ma et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 2005), and that the hindbrain rln3a neuronal clusters correspond to the NI (Donizetti et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Donizetti et al., 2008

claim: The zebrafish griseum centrale is a proposed target of the habenulo-interpeduncular nucleus (Hb-IPN) axis.
source: The zebrafish griseum centrale is a proposed target of the habenulo-interpeduncular nucleus (Hb-IPN) axis, a highly conserved forebrain to midbrain pathway implicated in modulating anxiety and the response to aversive stimuli (Agetsuma et al., 2010; Duboué et al., 2017; Facchin et al., 2015; McLaughlin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Agetsuma et al., 2010; Duboué et al., 2017; Facchin et al., 2015; McLaughlin et al., 2017

claim: The habenulo-interpeduncular nucleus (Hb-IPN) axis is a highly conserved forebrain to midbrain pathway implicated in modulating anxiety and the response to aversive stimuli.
source: The zebrafish griseum centrale is a proposed target of the habenulo-interpeduncular nucleus (Hb-IPN) axis, a highly conserved forebrain to midbrain pathway implicated in modulating anxiety and the response to aversive stimuli (Agetsuma et al., 2010; Duboué et al., 2017; Facchin et al., 2015; McLaughlin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Agetsuma et al., 2010; Duboué et al., 2017; Facchin et al., 2015; McLaughlin et al., 2017

claim: Left-right asymmetry of the habenular region is widespread among vertebrate species.
source: Left-right asymmetry of the habenular region is widespread among vertebrate species (Concha and Wilson, 2001; Harris et al., 1996) and in zebrafish the left and right dorsal habenulae (LdHb and RdHb) exhibit prominent differences in their molecular properties, connectivity, and functions (Agetsuma et al., 2010; Chou et al., 2016; deCarvalho et al., 2014; Dreosti et al., 2014; Duboué et al., 2017; Facchin et al., 2015; Gamse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Concha and Wilson, 2001; Harris et al., 1996

claim: In zebrafish the left and right dorsal habenulae (LdHb and RdHb) exhibit prominent differences in their molecular properties, connectivity, and functions.
source: Left-right asymmetry of the habenular region is widespread among vertebrate species (Concha and Wilson, 2001; Harris et al., 1996) and in zebrafish the left and right dorsal habenulae (LdHb and RdHb) exhibit prominent differences in their molecular properties, connectivity, and functions (Agetsuma et al., 2010; Chou et al., 2016; deCarvalho et al., 2014; Dreosti et al., 2014; Duboué et al., 2017; Facchin et al., 2015; Gamse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Agetsuma et al., 2010; Chou et al., 2016; deCarvalho et al., 2014; Dreosti et al., 2014; Duboué et al., 2017; Facchin et al., 2015; Gamse et al., 2005

claim: The LdHb projects to the dorsal IPN (dIPN) and ventral IPN (vIPN).
source: The LdHb projects to the dorsal IPN (dIPN) and ventral IPN (vIPN), whereas RdHb neurons largely innervate the vIPN (Gamse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gamse et al., 2005

claim: RdHb neurons largely innervate the vIPN.
source: The LdHb projects to the dorsal IPN (dIPN) and ventral IPN (vIPN), whereas RdHb neurons largely innervate the vIPN (Gamse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gamse et al., 2005

claim: vIPN neurons project to the dorsal raphe.
source: Using tract tracing in adult zebrafish, Agetsuma et al., 2010 found that vIPN neurons project to the dorsal raphe and dIPN neurons to the hindbrain griseum centrale.
evidence: Supported by citation to Agetsuma et al., 2010

claim: dIPN neurons project to the hindbrain griseum centrale.
source: Using tract tracing in adult zebrafish, Agetsuma et al., 2010 found that vIPN neurons project to the dorsal raphe and dIPN neurons to the hindbrain griseum centrale.
evidence: Supported by citation to Agetsuma et al., 2010

claim: Injection of neurobiotin into the dorsal IPN resulted in labeling of cell bodies in the griseum centrale, suggesting reciprocal connectivity.
source: Moreover, injection of the cell-filling dye neurobiotin into the dorsal IPN resulted in labeling of cell bodies in the griseum centrale, suggesting reciprocal connectivity (Agetsuma et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Agetsuma et al., 2010

claim: The NI and IPN are reciprocally connected in rodents.
source: The NI and IPN are also reciprocally connected in rodents (Goto et al., 2001; Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goto et al., 2001; Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003

claim: gsc2 transcripts were identified as enriched approximately fivefold in the IPN region relative to the rest of the brain.
source: After comparing the transcriptional profile of pooled IPN samples with remaining brain tissue, gsc2 transcripts were identified as enriched approximately fivefold in the IPN region relative to the rest of the brain.
evidence: Supported by transcriptional profiling data

claim: The gsc2 gene encodes a protein that has homology to Goosecoid-related proteins in its homeobox domain-containing sequence.
source: The gsc2 gene encodes a protein that has homology to Goosecoid-related proteins in its homeobox domain-containing sequence.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis

claim: The gsc2 sequence is not annotated in the latest genome assembly (GRCz11).
source: We note that the gsc2 sequence is not annotated in the latest genome assembly (GRCz11) and was initially identified by aligning reads to Zv9 (Ensembl release 77).
evidence: Based on genome database information

claim: gsc2 transcripts are restricted to bilateral clusters just posterior to the midbrain-hindbrain boundary and to a few sparsely distributed neurons anterior to the main cluster.
source: From whole-mount in situ hybridization (WISH), we found that gsc2 transcripts are restricted to bilateral clusters just posterior to the midbrain-hindbrain boundary and to a few sparsely distributed neurons anterior to the main cluster (Figure 1A and A').
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A and A'

claim: The bilateral gsc2 clusters are not situated within the IPN but rather lie dorsal to it.
source: Double labeling with somatostatin 1.1 (sst1.1), a marker of IPN neurons (Doll et al., 2011), revealed that the bilateral clusters are not situated within the IPN but rather lie dorsal to it (Figure 1B and B').
evidence: Supported by double-label in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1B and B'

claim: gsc2 neurons are a distinct population, located anterior to the rln3a neurons.
source: Owing to the similar positions of gsc2 and rln3a (Donizetti et al., 2008) neurons in the larval hindbrain, we performed double-label WISH, and found that gsc2 neurons are a distinct population, located anterior to the rln3a neurons (Figure 1C, C' and D).
evidence: Supported by double-label in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1C, C' and D

claim: Only cckb and nmbb transcripts were detected in the NI.
source: To determine whether transcripts encoding each of these neuropeptides are present in the zebrafish NI, we performed WISH for the zebrafish cholecystokinin a (ccka), cholecystokinin b (cckb), neuromedin a (nmba), neuromedin b (nmbb), and neurotensin (nts) genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E'). For cholecystokinin and neuromedin B, the combined expression of the two zebrafish paralogues closely resembles the overall expression pattern of each single rodent gene (Albus, 1988; Ohki-Hamazaki, 2000). Only cckb and nmbb transcripts were detected in the NI, and nmbb expression was also observed in the PAG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: nmbb expression was also observed in the PAG.
source: Only cckb and nmbb transcripts were detected in the NI, and nmbb expression was also observed in the PAG (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, D).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, D

claim: gsc2 neurons fail to express any of the neuropeptides ccka, cckb, nmba, nmbb, or nts.
source: Using double-label fluorescent WISH, we found that the gsc2 neurons (48.33±2.33 neurons) fail to express any of these neuropeptides and comprise a unique population.
evidence: Supported by double-label fluorescent in situ hybridization data

claim: gsc2 neurons comprise 48.33±2.33 neurons.
source: Using double-label fluorescent WISH, we found that the gsc2 neurons (48.33±2.33 neurons) fail to express any of these neuropeptides and comprise a unique population.
evidence: Supported by cell counting data

claim: Hindbrain nmbb neurons comprise 8.33±1.45 neurons.
source: We found that hindbrain nmbb neurons (8.33±1.45) are intermingled with rln3a neurons (10.67±1.33) in the NI, with a small subset expressing both neuropeptides (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A'-C'').
evidence: Supported by cell counting data

claim: rln3a neurons comprise 10.67±1.33 neurons in the NI.
source: We found that hindbrain nmbb neurons (8.33±1.45) are intermingled with rln3a neurons (10.67±1.33) in the NI, with a small subset expressing both neuropeptides (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A'-C'').
evidence: Supported by cell counting data

claim: Hindbrain nmbb neurons are intermingled with rln3a neurons in the NI, with a small subset expressing both neuropeptides.
source: We found that hindbrain nmbb neurons (8.33±1.45) are intermingled with rln3a neurons (10.67±1.33) in the NI, with a small subset expressing both neuropeptides (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A'-C'').
evidence: Supported by double-label fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A'-C''

claim: rln3a and nmbb neurons exist as separate, adjacent populations in the PAG.
source: By contrast, rln3a and nmbb neurons exist as separate, adjacent populations in the PAG (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by double-label fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Hindbrain cckb neurons comprise 4.5±1.1 neurons.
source: Hindbrain cckb neurons (4.5±1.1) are a distinct population located just posterior to rln3a and nmbb neurons (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by cell counting data

claim: Hindbrain cckb neurons are a distinct population located just posterior to rln3a and nmbb neurons.
source: Hindbrain cckb neurons (4.5±1.1) are a distinct population located just posterior to rln3a and nmbb neurons (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by double-label fluorescent in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Tg(gsc2:QF2)c721 was generated by introducing the QF2 sequence into exon 2 of the gsc2 gene through non-homologous end joining.
source: Tg(gsc2:QF2)c721 was generated by introducing the QF2 sequence into exon 2 of the gsc2 gene through non-homologous end joining (Kimura et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the transgenic line

claim: Tg(rln3a:QF2, he1.1:YFP)c836 was generated by integrating QF2 and a secondary reporter into exon 1 of the rln3a gene using GeneWeld.
source: Another method for homology-directed integration called GeneWeld (Wierson et al., 2020) was adapted to include a secondary reporter that, together with the QF2 sequence, was integrated into exon 1 of the rln3a gene to produce Tg(rln3a:QF2, he1.1:YFP)c836.
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the transgenic line

claim: The Tg(gsc2:QF2)c721 driver line recapitulates endogenous expression patterns of gsc2 at both larval and adult stages.
source: We confirmed that the Tg(gsc2:QF2)c721 and Tg(rln3a:QF2, he1.1:YFP)c836 driver lines recapitulate endogenous expression patterns of gsc2 and rln3a, respectively, at both larval (Figure 2B, C, E and F) and adult (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–G) stages.
evidence: Supported by comparison of transgene expression with in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2

claim: The Tg(rln3a:QF2, he1.1:YFP)c836 driver line recapitulates endogenous expression patterns of rln3a at both larval and adult stages.
source: We confirmed that the Tg(gsc2:QF2)c721 and Tg(rln3a:QF2, he1.1:YFP)c836 driver lines recapitulate endogenous expression patterns of gsc2 and rln3a, respectively, at both larval (Figure 2B, C, E and F) and adult (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–G) stages.
evidence: Supported by comparison of transgene expression with in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2

claim: The rln3a and gsc2 neurons reside on the floor of the 4th ventricle.
source: Consistent with their location in the NI, the rln3a and gsc2 neurons reside on the floor of the 4th ventricle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), with the gsc2 neurons anterior to the rln3a neurons and also distributed more ventrally up to the dorsal surface of the raphe nucleus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: gsc2 neurons are anterior to the rln3a neurons and also distributed more ventrally up to the dorsal surface of the raphe nucleus.
source: Consistent with their location in the NI, the rln3a and gsc2 neurons reside on the floor of the 4th ventricle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), with the gsc2 neurons anterior to the rln3a neurons and also distributed more ventrally up to the dorsal surface of the raphe nucleus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: gsc2 neurons are located outside of the IPN in the adult brain.
source: Using TgBAC(gng8:Eco.NfsB-2A-CAAX-GFP)c375 to delineate dHb axon terminals at the IPN (deCarvalho et al., 2013), we confirmed that gsc2 neurons are located outside of the IPN in the adult brain, although a few scattered gsc2 neurons lie just posterior and lateral to it (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D').
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D'

claim: A few scattered gsc2 neurons lie just posterior and lateral to the IPN.
source: Using TgBAC(gng8:Eco.NfsB-2A-CAAX-GFP)c375 to delineate dHb axon terminals at the IPN (deCarvalho et al., 2013), we confirmed that gsc2 neurons are located outside of the IPN in the adult brain, although a few scattered gsc2 neurons lie just posterior and lateral to it (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D').
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D'

claim: In mice, the NI contains a large population of GABAergic neurons.
source: In mice (Szőnyi et al., 2019) and rats (Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003), the NI contains a large population of GABAergic neurons, and rln3a NI neurons are largely GABAergic (Ma et al., 2007; Nasirova et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Szőnyi et al., 2019

claim: In rats, the NI contains a large population of GABAergic neurons.
source: In mice (Szőnyi et al., 2019) and rats (Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003), the NI contains a large population of GABAergic neurons, and rln3a NI neurons are largely GABAergic (Ma et al., 2007; Nasirova et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003

claim: rln3a NI neurons are largely GABAergic.
source: In mice (Szőnyi et al., 2019) and rats (Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003), the NI contains a large population of GABAergic neurons, and rln3a NI neurons are largely GABAergic (Ma et al., 2007; Nasirova et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2007; Nasirova et al., 2020

claim: gsc2 neurons do not co-express with the glutamatergic reporter in the NI.
source: We did not observe co-expression of gsc2 (Figure 3A) or rln3a (Figure 3C) with the glutamatergic reporter in the NI.
evidence: Supported by double-labeling data shown in Figure 3A

claim: rln3a neurons do not co-express with the glutamatergic reporter in the NI.
source: We did not observe co-expression of gsc2 (Figure 3A) or rln3a (Figure 3C) with the glutamatergic reporter in the NI.
evidence: Supported by double-labeling data shown in Figure 3C

claim: An average of 82.43±3.52% of gsc2 neurons co-expressed GFP and mApple-CAAX in TgBac(gad1b:GFP)nns25; Tg(gsc2:QF2)c721; Tg(QUAS:mApple-CAAX, he1.1:mCherry)c636 larvae.
source: In contrast, an average of 82.43±3.52% of neurons co-expressed GFP and mApple-CAAX in TgBac(gad1b:GFP)nns25; Tg(gsc2:QF2)c721; Tg(QUAS:mApple-CAAX, he1.1:mCherry)c636 larvae (Figure 3D, D' and G).
evidence: Supported by double-labeling data shown in Figure 3D, D' and G

claim: An average of 80.57±5.57% of rln3a NI neurons co-expressed GFP and mApple in TgBac(gad1b:GFP)nns25; Tg(rln3a:QF2, he1.1:YFP)c836; Tg(QUAS:mApple, he1.1:CFP)c788 larvae.
source: Similarly, in TgBac(gad1b:GFP)nns25; Tg(rln3a:QF2, he1.1:YFP)c836; Tg(QUAS:mApple, he1.1:CFP)c788 larvae, an average of 80.57±5.57% of neurons co-expressed GFP and mApple (Figure 3F, F', F'' and G).
evidence: Supported by double-labeling data shown in Figure 3F, F', F'' and G

claim: gsc2 and rln3a neurons are predominantly GABAergic.
source: These results indicate that gsc2 and rln3a neurons are predominantly GABAergic, consistent with their NI identity.
evidence: Inferred from the co-expression data with GABAergic markers

claim: rln3a neurons in the PAG were not labeled by the glutamatergic reporter.
source: We found that rln3a neurons in the PAG were not labeled by the glutamatergic reporter (Figure 3B), whereas an average of 81.67±3.81% showed labeling from the gad1b transgene (Figure 3E, E', E'' and G).
evidence: Supported by double-labeling data shown in Figure 3B

claim: An average of 81.67±3.81% of rln3a PAG neurons showed labeling from the gad1b transgene.
source: We found that rln3a neurons in the PAG were not labeled by the glutamatergic reporter (Figure 3B), whereas an average of 81.67±3.81% showed labeling from the gad1b transgene (Figure 3E, E', E'' and G).
evidence: Supported by double-labeling data shown in Figure 3E, E', E'' and G

claim: rln3a neurons possess similar neurotransmitter identity across neuroanatomical locations.
source: This suggests that rln3a neurons possess similar neurotransmitter identity across neuroanatomical locations.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that both NI and PAG rln3a neurons are GABAergic

claim: At 6 dpf, projections from gsc2 neurons were prominent in the cerebellum, IPN, raphe, diencephalon, and rostral and caudal hypothalamus.
source: At 6 dpf, projections from gsc2 neurons were prominent in the cerebellum, IPN, raphe, diencephalon, and rostral and caudal hypothalamus (Figure 4—video 1, Figure 4A–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, B').
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 4

claim: Sparse efferents from gsc2 neurons were found in the medulla and telencephalon.
source: Sparse efferents from gsc2 neurons were also found in the medulla (Figure 4—video 1) and telencephalon (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 4

claim: Projections from rln3a neurons were found in the medulla, IPN, diencephalon, lateral hypothalamus, and optic tectum.
source: Projections from rln3a neurons were found in the medulla, IPN, diencephalon, lateral hypothalamus, and optic tectum (Figure 4—video 2, Figure 4F–J), with some axons appearing to pass through the posterior commissure (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 4

claim: Some rln3a axons appear to pass through the posterior commissure.
source: Projections from rln3a neurons were found in the medulla, IPN, diencephalon, lateral hypothalamus, and optic tectum (Figure 4—video 2, Figure 4F–J), with some axons appearing to pass through the posterior commissure (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 4G

claim: Sparse rln3a fibers were observed in the raphe and telencephalon.
source: Sparse fibers were also observed in the raphe and telencephalon (Figure 4H and J).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 4H and J

claim: Innervation of the IPN by rln3a neurons originates solely from the NI cluster.
source: Innervation of the IPN by rln3a neurons originates solely from the NI cluster, whereas the bulk of projections throughout the brain emanate from rln3a neurons in the PAG (Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: Supported by ablation experiments shown in Figure 4K-M

claim: The bulk of rln3a projections throughout the brain emanate from rln3a neurons in the PAG.
source: Innervation of the IPN by rln3a neurons originates solely from the NI cluster, whereas the bulk of projections throughout the brain emanate from rln3a neurons in the PAG (Figure 4—video 2).
evidence: Supported by ablation experiments shown in Figure 4K-M

claim: Ablation of rln3a PAG neurons greatly reduced fibers in the medulla, diencephalon, hypothalamus and optic tectum, but spared innervation of the IPN.
source: This was confirmed by two-photon laser ablation of rln3a PAG neurons, which greatly reduced fibers in the medulla, diencephalon, hypothalamus and optic tectum, but spared innervation of the IPN (Figure 4K–M).
evidence: Supported by ablation data shown in Figure 4K-M

claim: rln3a NI neurons exclusively target the IPN.
source: Reduction of rln3a PAG neuronal projections enabled visualization of those from the NI, which exclusively target the IPN (Figure 4—video 3, Figure 4L).
evidence: Supported by ablation data shown in Figure 4L

claim: Ablation of rln3a neurons solely in the NI eliminated innervation of the IPN without affecting the rest of the rln3a neuron projection pattern.
source: Accordingly, ablation of rln3a neurons solely in the NI eliminated innervation of the IPN without affecting the rest of the rln3a neuron projection pattern, including projections to the medulla, diencephalon, hypothalamus and optic tectum (Figure 4M).
evidence: Supported by ablation data shown in Figure 4M

claim: Efferents from gsc2 neurons were far more extensive than those of rln3a NI neurons.
source: Efferents from gsc2 neurons were far more extensive than those of rln3a NI neurons, and were observed in regions not innervated by any rln3a neurons (e.g. cerebellum and caudal hypothalamus).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of projection patterns shown in Figure 4

claim: gsc2 efferents were observed in regions not innervated by any rln3a neurons (e.g. cerebellum and caudal hypothalamus).
source: Efferents from gsc2 neurons were far more extensive than those of rln3a NI neurons, and were observed in regions not innervated by any rln3a neurons (e.g. cerebellum and caudal hypothalamus).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 4

claim: The closely apposed gsc2 and rln3a NI neurons exhibit divergent and largely non-overlapping projection patterns.
source: Thus, the closely apposed gsc2 and rln3a NI neurons exhibit divergent and largely non-overlapping projection patterns.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of projection patterns shown in Figure 4

claim: gsc2 and rln3a neuronal cell bodies are located dorsal to the IPN.
source: We confirmed the location of gsc2 and rln3a neuronal cell bodies dorsal to the IPN as visualized by nuclear-tagged reporters (Figure 5A, A', and C, C').
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5A, A', C, C'

claim: Both gsc2 and rln3a populations project to the IPN.
source: Using membrane-tagged reporters, we identified projections from both populations to the IPN (Figure 5B, D and E–H) and found that they innervate disparate regions.
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5

claim: gsc2 and rln3a neurons innervate disparate regions of the IPN.
source: Using membrane-tagged reporters, we identified projections from both populations to the IPN (Figure 5B, D and E–H) and found that they innervate disparate regions.
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5

claim: Axons of gsc2 neurons terminate at the ventral IPN mainly along the midline neuropil.
source: This is more readily observed in sections of the adult brain in which axons of gsc2 neurons terminate at the ventral IPN mainly along the midline neuropil (Figure 5B, E–F', I) and axons of rln3a neurons terminate at the dorsal IPN (Figure 5D, G–H', J), as depicted schematically in Figure 5K.
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5B, E–F', I

claim: Axons of rln3a neurons terminate at the dorsal IPN.
source: This is more readily observed in sections of the adult brain in which axons of gsc2 neurons terminate at the ventral IPN mainly along the midline neuropil (Figure 5B, E–F', I) and axons of rln3a neurons terminate at the dorsal IPN (Figure 5D, G–H', J), as depicted schematically in Figure 5K.
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5D, G–H', J

claim: Tracing studies in mice, rats, and zebrafish suggest that NI neurons receive afferent input from the Hb-IPN pathway.
source: Tracing studies in mice (Lu et al., 2020), rats (Goto et al., 2001; Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003), and zebrafish (Agetsuma et al., 2010) suggest that NI neurons receive afferent input from the Hb-IPN pathway.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2020; Goto et al., 2001; Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003; Agetsuma et al., 2010

claim: Activation of the dHb-IPN axis increases activity in gsc2 neurons.
source: These results show that activation of the dHb-IPN axis increases activity in gsc2 neurons but not in rln3a neurons, indicating that the latter do not directly mediate functions of the dHb-IPN pathway.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation and calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6

claim: Activation of the dHb-IPN axis does not increase activity in rln3a neurons.
source: These results show that activation of the dHb-IPN axis increases activity in gsc2 neurons but not in rln3a neurons, indicating that the latter do not directly mediate functions of the dHb-IPN pathway.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic activation and calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6

claim: rln3a neurons do not directly mediate functions of the dHb-IPN pathway.
source: These results show that activation of the dHb-IPN axis increases activity in gsc2 neurons but not in rln3a neurons, indicating that the latter do not directly mediate functions of the dHb-IPN pathway.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of response to dHb activation

claim: In rodents, aversive stimuli increase neuronal activity in the NI.
source: In rodents, aversive stimuli, such as foot shock, air puff, water-restraint stress, exposure to an elevated plus maze, and the anxiogenic drug FG-7142 all increase neuronal activity in the NI ( Lawther et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2020; Passerin et al., 2000; Rajkumar et al., 2016; Szőnyi et al., 2019; Tanaka et al., 2005), yet whether NI neuronal subtypes show distinct responses to aversive stimuli is unclear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lawther et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2020; Passerin et al., 2000; Rajkumar et al., 2016; Szőnyi et al., 2019; Tanaka et al., 2005

claim: gsc2 neurons showed little spontaneous activity and a robust increase in calcium signaling in response to shock.
source: The gsc2 neurons showed little spontaneous activity and a robust increase in calcium signaling in response to shock (Figure 7D and D', Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7D and D'

claim: rln3a neurons showed more spontaneous fluctuations in activity throughout the recording period.
source: By contrast, rln3a neurons showed more spontaneous fluctuations in activity throughout the recording period (Figure 7E–H, Figure 7—video 1), producing a wider distribution of amplitudes (Figure 7F–G'), and their response to shock was shorter in duration than for gsc2 neurons (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7E–H

claim: rln3a neurons produce a wider distribution of calcium signal amplitudes than gsc2 neurons.
source: By contrast, rln3a neurons showed more spontaneous fluctuations in activity throughout the recording period (Figure 7E–H, Figure 7—video 1), producing a wider distribution of amplitudes (Figure 7F–G'), and their response to shock was shorter in duration than for gsc2 neurons (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7F–G'

claim: The response to shock was shorter in duration for rln3a neurons than for gsc2 neurons.
source: By contrast, rln3a neurons showed more spontaneous fluctuations in activity throughout the recording period (Figure 7E–H, Figure 7—video 1), producing a wider distribution of amplitudes (Figure 7F–G'), and their response to shock was shorter in duration than for gsc2 neurons (Figure 7I).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7I

claim: The gsc2 and rln3a neurons differ in their spontaneous activity and in the duration of their response to an aversive stimulus.
source: The gsc2 and rln3a neurons therefore differ in their spontaneous activity and in the duration of their response to an aversive stimulus.
evidence: Inferred from calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7

claim: Rodent studies found decreased voluntary wheel running in animals with null mutations in the gene encoding RLN3 or its receptor RXFP3.
source: Rodent studies have described the behavior of animals with null mutations in the gene encoding RLN3 (Smith et al., 2012), or its receptor, RXFP3 (Hosken et al., 2015), and found decreased voluntary wheel running, suggesting that the relaxin-3 system is involved in regulating locomotor activity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Smith et al., 2012; Hosken et al., 2015

claim: The relaxin-3 system is involved in regulating locomotor activity.
source: Rodent studies have described the behavior of animals with null mutations in the gene encoding RLN3 (Smith et al., 2012), or its receptor, RXFP3 (Hosken et al., 2015), and found decreased voluntary wheel running, suggesting that the relaxin-3 system is involved in regulating locomotor activity.
evidence: Inferred from mutant phenotypes described in citations

claim: Activation of the NI through microstimulation or chemogenetics increased movement in rats.
source: Activation of the NI through microstimulation or chemogenetics increased movement in rats (Farooq et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2017), which implicates the NI region in regulating locomotor activity but does not identify the relevant neurons.
evidence: Supported by citations to Farooq et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2017

claim: Removal of rln3a NI neurons elicited hyperactivity in zebrafish larvae.
source: Strikingly, removal of rln3a NI neurons elicited hyperactivity in zebrafish larvae.
evidence: Supported by ablation and behavioral data shown in Figure 8

claim: Ablation of rln3a neurons in the PAG did not affect locomotion.
source: Ablation of rln3a neurons in the PAG did not affect locomotion.
evidence: Supported by ablation and behavioral data shown in Figure 8

claim: The role of the NI in regulating baseline locomotor activity is mediated by rln3a neurons.
source: This suggests that the role of the NI in regulating baseline locomotor activity is mediated by rln3a neurons.
evidence: Inferred from ablation experiments showing that only rln3a NI neuron ablation affects locomotion

claim: NI neurons normally suppress spontaneous locomotor activity in larval zebrafish.
source: Previous studies in adult rodents indicate that enhanced NI activity promotes locomotion, but we find the opposite in larval zebrafish; NI neurons normally suppress spontaneous locomotor activity.
evidence: Inferred from the hyperactivity observed after ablation of rln3a NI neurons

claim: Dopamine suppressed spontaneous fictive swim episodes in larval zebrafish.
source: Interestingly, a study of dopaminergic signaling in larval zebrafish also reported that dopamine suppressed spontaneous fictive swim episodes (Thirumalai and Cline, 2008), although dopamine is classically known for stimulating locomotor activity in adult rodents (Ryczko and Dubuc, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thirumalai and Cline, 2008

claim: Dopamine is classically known for stimulating locomotor activity in adult rodents.
source: Interestingly, a study of dopaminergic signaling in larval zebrafish also reported that dopamine suppressed spontaneous fictive swim episodes (Thirumalai and Cline, 2008), although dopamine is classically known for stimulating locomotor activity in adult rodents (Ryczko and Dubuc, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ryczko and Dubuc, 2017

claim: Differential roles for neuromodulators during development and adulthood could be a general feature of locomotor circuitry.
source: Thus, differential roles for neuromodulators during development and adulthood could be a general feature of locomotor circuitry.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences between larval and adult effects

claim: Aversive stimuli promote expression of c-Fos in the NI.
source: A number of studies have found that aversive stimuli promote expression of c-Fos in the NI (Lawther et al., 2015; Passerin et al., 2000; Rajkumar et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2005), leading researchers to evaluate the role of relaxin-3 in anxiety-like behaviors.
evidence: Supported by citations to Lawther et al., 2015; Passerin et al., 2000; Rajkumar et al., 2016; Tanaka et al., 2005

claim: In rats, intracerebroventricular infusion of a relaxin-3 receptor agonist increases entries to the open arms of an elevated plus maze and the amount of time animals spend in the light portion of a light-dark box.
source: In rats, intracerebroventricular infusion of a relaxin-3 receptor agonist increases entries to the open arms of an elevated plus maze and the amount of time animals spend in the light portion of a light-dark box (Ryan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ryan et al., 2013

claim: In mice, the relaxin-3 receptor agonist did not alter the basal behavioral state but reduced anxiety-like behavior induced by the anxiogenic drug FG-7142.
source: Similar assays in mice showed that the relaxin-3 receptor agonist did not alter the basal behavioral state but rather reduced anxiety-like behavior induced by the anxiogenic drug FG-7142 (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015

claim: Nmb neurons in the mouse NI promote spontaneous locomotor activity and are activated in response to foot shock.
source: Lu et al., 2020 note that Nmb neurons in the mouse NI promote spontaneous locomotor activity and are activated in response to foot shock, a stimulus that elicits immediate locomotion, but whether they mediate the immediate locomotor response to this stimulus is unclear.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2020

claim: Loss of either NI rln3a or gsc2 neurons was not sufficient to alter hyperactivity normally observed in zebrafish larvae post-shock.
source: Through selective ablation, we found that loss of either NI rln3a or gsc2 neurons was not sufficient to alter hyperactivity normally observed in zebrafish larvae post-shock.
evidence: Supported by ablation and behavioral data shown in Figure 8

claim: Zebrafish hindbrain rln3a neurons localize to a region expressing corticotropin releasing hormone receptor 1 (crhr1).
source: Previous work showed that zebrafish hindbrain rln3a neurons localize to a region expressing corticotropin releasing hormone receptor 1 (crhr1), which encodes a receptor expressed at high levels in the rodent NI (Bittencourt and Sawchenko, 2000, Potter et al., 1994; ).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bittencourt and Sawchenko, 2000, Potter et al., 1994

claim: Transcripts encoding neuromedin B and cholecystokinin map to the presumptive zebrafish NI.
source: We find that transcripts encoding neuromedin B and cholecystokinin, which have also been detected in the rodent NI (Kubota et al., 1983; Lu et al., 2020; Olucha-Bordonau et al., 2003), likewise map to the presumptive zebrafish NI.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1

claim: In mice, Rln3 and Nmb are expressed in interspersed neuronal populations and are co-expressed in a subset of cells.
source: Similar to rln3a and nmbb neurons in the zebrafish larval NI, in mice Rln3 and Nmb are expressed in interspersed neuronal populations and are co-expressed in a subset of cells (Lu et al., 2020; Nasirova et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2020; Nasirova et al., 2020

claim: cckb neurons are a separate population located posterior to the rln3a and nmbb neurons.
source: Furthermore, we found that cckb neurons are a separate population located posterior to the rln3a and nmbb neurons.
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1

claim: There is little overlap between cholecystokinin and relaxin-3 neurons in the rat brain.
source: Szlaga et al., 2022 also found little overlap between cholecystokinin and relaxin-3 neurons in the rat brain.
evidence: Supported by citation to Szlaga et al., 2022

claim: These results suggest conservation of NI cell types and their organization from fish to mammals.
source: Together, these results suggest conservation of NI cell types and their organization from fish to mammals, establishing zebrafish as a model to understand the connectivity and function of the diverse types of NI neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the similarities in neuropeptide expression patterns across species

claim: A new study identified a region in the zebrafish larval hindbrain, referred to as the dorsal tegmental nucleus, whose GABAergic neurons project to the dorsal IPN and are activated in conjunction with directional turning by the larva.
source: Intriguingly, a new study identified a region in the zebrafish larval hindbrain, referred to as the dorsal tegmental nucleus, whose GABAergic neurons project to the dorsal IPN and are activated in conjunction with directional turning by the larva (Petrucco et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Petrucco et al., 2023

claim: The dorsal tegmental nucleus neurons likely correspond to a subpopulation in the NI.
source: Although the specific neuronal cell types have yet to be identified, it is likely they correspond to a subpopulation in the NI.
evidence: This is speculation based on the anatomical and functional similarities

claim: Larvae that lacked rln3a NI neurons swam a greater overall distance during the pre-shock period than unablated controls, larvae with ablated gsc2 neurons, or larvae with ablated rln3a PAG neurons.
source: Unexpectedly, however, larvae that lacked rln3a NI neurons swam a greater overall distance during the pre-shock period and exhibited longer phases of activity than unablated controls, larvae with ablated gsc2 neurons, or larvae with ablated rln3a PAG neurons (Figure 8F–H, Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8F–H

claim: Larvae that lacked rln3a NI neurons exhibited longer phases of activity than unablated controls, larvae with ablated gsc2 neurons, or larvae with ablated rln3a PAG neurons.
source: Unexpectedly, however, larvae that lacked rln3a NI neurons swam a greater overall distance during the pre-shock period and exhibited longer phases of activity than unablated controls, larvae with ablated gsc2 neurons, or larvae with ablated rln3a PAG neurons (Figure 8F–H, Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8F–H

claim: Ablation of rln3a NI neurons promotes prolonged phases of movement, rather than increasing the frequency of movement initiation.
source: This indicates that ablation of rln3a NI neurons promotes prolonged phases of movement, rather than increasing the frequency of movement initiation.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that phase length increased but phase number did not

claim: Larvae that lacked rln3a NI neurons showed increased turning behavior.
source: In addition to increased swimming, larvae that lacked rln3a NI neurons showed increased turning behavior.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8-figure supplement 2

claim: For larvae with ablated rln3a NI neurons, the change in angle of orientation measured per unit of distance traveled was greater than that of unablated controls, larvae with ablated gsc2 neurons, or larvae with ablated rln3a PAG neurons.
source: For larvae with ablated rln3a NI neurons, the change in angle of orientation measured per unit of distance traveled was greater than that of unablated controls, larvae with ablated gsc2 neurons, or larvae with ablated rln3a PAG neurons (Figure 8-figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8-figure supplement 2A

claim: Spontaneous locomotor activity and turning behavior are increased following ablation of the rln3a cluster of NI neurons.
source: Overall, the results show that spontaneous locomotor activity and turning behavior are increased following ablation of the rln3a cluster of NI neurons, whereas swimming behavior is normal after ablation of the larger gsc2 population.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8

claim: Swimming behavior is normal after ablation of the larger gsc2 population.
source: Overall, the results show that spontaneous locomotor activity and turning behavior are increased following ablation of the rln3a cluster of NI neurons, whereas swimming behavior is normal after ablation of the larger gsc2 population.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 8

claim: The IPN could integrate signals from disparate neuronal populations in the dHb and NI, and perhaps other brain regions.
source: The IPN could thus integrate signals from disparate neuronal populations in the dHb and NI, and perhaps other brain regions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the anatomical connectivity patterns

claim: Relaxin-3 neurons fire in synchrony with the ascending phase of the hippocampal theta oscillation (4–12 Hz) in rats.
source: A study in rats found that relaxin-3 neurons fire in synchrony with the ascending phase of the hippocampal theta oscillation (4–12 Hz), which has been implicated in spatial memory (Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma et al., 2013

claim: Stimulation of NI neurons in rats and Nmb NI neurons in mice increases hippocampal theta power.
source: Stimulation of NI neurons in rats and Nmb NI neurons in mice also increases hippocampal theta power (Lu et al., 2020; Nuñez et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 2020; Nuñez et al., 2006

claim: The oscillating calcium transients detected in rln3a neurons of larval zebrafish are on the order of seconds.
source: The oscillating calcium transients that we detected in rln3a neurons of larval zebrafish are on the order of seconds; however, consistent with infra-slow waves that occur at frequencies in the range of tens to hundreds of seconds, and within which fast oscillations are often nested (Palva and Palva, 2012).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7

claim: Infra-slow oscillations correlate with rhythmic fluctuations in performance observed in psychophysical experiments with humans.
source: Infra-slow oscillations correlate with rhythmic fluctuations in performance observed in psychophysical experiments with humans, in which a subject performs a task of constant difficulty for several minutes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Palva and Palva, 2012

claim: Intra-slow waves coordinate shifts between attentive and inattentive brain states.
source: It has been proposed, therefore, that intra-slow waves coordinate shifts between attentive and inattentive brain states (Palva and Palva, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Palva and Palva, 2012

claim: Fluctuating activity in rln3a neurons may control transitions between phases of behavioral activity and inactivity.
source: Given that ablation of rln3a NI neurons increases the length of phases of movement in zebrafish larvae, fluctuating activity in rln3a neurons may control transitions between phases of behavioral activity and inactivity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed effects of ablation

claim: Gsc2 neurons in the mouse brain have been identified, although there is conflicting information about their precise anatomical location.
source: Neurons expressing the Gsc2 murine homolog had previously been identified in the mouse brain, although there is conflicting information about their precise anatomical location (Funato et al., 2010; Gong et al., 2003; Gottlieb et al., 1998 Saint-Jore et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Funato et al., 2010; Gong et al., 2003; Gottlieb et al., 1998 Saint-Jore et al., 1998

claim: Gsc2 neurons are likely not located within the rodent IPN but are likely situated adjacent to it.
source: On the basis of our results, we suspect that Gsc2 neurons are not located within the rodent IPN as was previously concluded (Funato et al., 2010; Gong et al., 2003), but are likely situated adjacent to it.
evidence: This is speculation based on the zebrafish data

claim: The anatomical location, neurotransmitter phenotype, and hodological properties of gsc2 and rln3a neurons are consistent with NI identity.
source: By labeling with QUAS-driven fluorescent reporters, we determined that the anatomical location, neurotransmitter phenotype, and hodological properties of gsc2 and rln3a neurons are consistent with NI identity, supporting the assertion that the griseum centrale of fish is analogous to the mammalian NI.
evidence: Supported by anatomical and molecular data shown in Figures 2-5

claim: The griseum centrale of fish is analogous to the mammalian NI.
source: By labeling with QUAS-driven fluorescent reporters, we determined that the anatomical location, neurotransmitter phenotype, and hodological properties of gsc2 and rln3a neurons are consistent with NI identity, supporting the assertion that the griseum centrale of fish is analogous to the mammalian NI.
evidence: Inferred from the similarities in anatomical location, neurotransmitter phenotype, and connectivity

claim: Both gsc2 and rln3a groups of neurons are GABAergic, reside on the floor of the fourth ventricle and project to the interpeduncular nucleus.
source: Both groups of neurons are GABAergic, reside on the floor of the fourth ventricle and project to the interpeduncular nucleus.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 5

claim: gsc2 and rln3a neuronal populations have distinct connections with the IPN and other brain regions.
source: However, these adjacent neuronal populations have distinct connections with the IPN and other brain regions, and also differ in their afferent input, calcium signaling, and influence on locomotor behavior (summarized in Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 4-8 and summarized in Table 1

claim: gsc2 and rln3a neuronal populations differ in their afferent input.
source: However, these adjacent neuronal populations have distinct connections with the IPN and other brain regions, and also differ in their afferent input, calcium signaling, and influence on locomotor behavior (summarized in Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and summarized in Table 1

claim: gsc2 and rln3a neuronal populations differ in their calcium signaling.
source: However, these adjacent neuronal populations have distinct connections with the IPN and other brain regions, and also differ in their afferent input, calcium signaling, and influence on locomotor behavior (summarized in Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7 and summarized in Table 1

claim: gsc2 and rln3a neuronal populations differ in their influence on locomotor behavior.
source: However, these adjacent neuronal populations have distinct connections with the IPN and other brain regions, and also differ in their afferent input, calcium signaling, and influence on locomotor behavior (summarized in Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8 and summarized in Table 1

claim: The NI has been proposed to act in concert with the median raphe and IPN, in 'a midline behavior control network of the brainstem'.
source: Owing that the NI has been proposed to act in concert with the median raphe and IPN, in 'a midline behavior control network of the brainstem' (Goto et al., 2001), it is important to build the framework of neuronal subtypes that mediate such coordinated activity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Goto et al., 2001

claim: Neurons in the left dHb project to both the dorsal IPN (dIPN) and ventral IPN (vIPN).
source: Previous work demonstrated that axons from left dHb and right dHb neurons innervate different regions along the dorsoventral extent of the IPN; neurons in the left dHb project to both the dorsal IPN (dIPN) and ventral IPN (vIPN), whereas right dHb neurons mainly target the vIPN (Gamse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gamse et al., 2005

claim: Right dHb neurons mainly target the vIPN.
source: Previous work demonstrated that axons from left dHb and right dHb neurons innervate different regions along the dorsoventral extent of the IPN; neurons in the left dHb project to both the dorsal IPN (dIPN) and ventral IPN (vIPN), whereas right dHb neurons mainly target the vIPN (Gamse et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gamse et al., 2005

claim: Different populations of NI neurons target specific IPN compartments; rln3a neurons project mainly to the dIPN and gsc2 neurons predominantly innervate the vIPN along its midline neuropil.
source: We found that different populations of NI neurons also target specific IPN compartments; rln3a neurons project mainly to the dIPN and gsc2 neurons predominantly innervate the vIPN along its midline neuropil.
evidence: Supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 5

claim: Spontaneous calcium spikes in cholinergic dHb terminals at the vIPN coincide with transient decreases in calcium signaling in non-cholinergic dHb terminals at the dIPN.
source: A study by Zaupa et al., 2021 demonstrates that axon terminals from cholinergic and noncholinergic dHb neurons, which innervate the vIPN and dIPN respectively, show distinct patterns of activity. Spontaneous calcium spikes in cholinergic dHb terminals at the vIPN coincide with transient decreases in calcium signaling in non-cholinergic dHb terminals at the dIPN.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zaupa et al., 2021

claim: Negatively correlated activity between cholinergic and non-cholinergic dHb terminals is mediated by activation of vIPN neurons that release GABA to inhibit non-cholinergic dHb terminals at the dIPN through their presynaptic GABAB receptors.
source: This negatively correlated activity is mediated by activation of vIPN neurons that release GABA to inhibit non-cholinergic dHb terminals at the dIPN through their presynaptic GABAB receptors.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zaupa et al., 2021
